title: Nvidia's Jensen Huang Says He Would Cut Off Customers Building Unsafe AI
excerpt: In a London interview, Nvidia's chief executive said he would halt chip supplies to a developer building unsafe AI — after talks first — while arguing that current safety fears are overstated and backing UK safety research with $250 million in computing resources.
body:
• Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang told Bloomberg in London that he would halt chip supplies to a customer developing unsafe AI software, but only after a direct conversation first.
  • Huang said Nvidia's technology is general-purpose and there are limits to the judgment it can apply to how other companies use its chips.
  • He argued the current level of concern about AI safety is not warranted, describing the fears as growing pains for a fast-expanding industry.
  • Nvidia will donate computing resources valued at $250 million over five years to UK research into agentic AI safety, including labs led by Oxford and UCL and work at Imperial College London.

Nvidia Chief Executive Officer Jensen Huang said he would halt the supply of chips to a customer that was developing unsafe AI software, even as he argued that the current level of concern about the technology is not warranted. Asked in an interview with Bloomberg's Emily Chang in London whether he would stop supplying an irresponsible developer, Huang gave a qualified yes.

"It's a hypothetical, but yes. But before you do so, you would have a conversation."

— Jensen Huang, CEO, Nvidia

Huang stressed the limits of that position. Nvidia does not run other companies, he said, and there is a limit to the judgment it applies to how customers use its technology, which he described as general-purpose. The remarks were made during a tour of Europe ahead of a company event in Berlin.

A Supplier at the Centre of the Safety Debate

Nvidia is the dominant supplier of AI accelerators, the chips used to train and run AI models, and that position has put the company at the centre of a debate over whether the software risks growing too powerful and slipping out of human control. AI executives such as Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei have proposed an industrywide slowdown to address those concerns. Scrutiny has also intensified after developers including Anthropic and OpenAI disclosed instances of rogue or undesired behaviour by AI agents, according to Reuters.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=nnwIi6547DU

Huang rejected the slowdown framing. He described the fears as growing pains for an industry expanding quickly, said some of the concern is self-imposed, and argued that the industry is doing a poor job of explaining the benefits of the technology. Young companies, he said, are growing incredibly fast and are still growing into the accountability and responsibility that come with building them.

AI as Its Own Safeguard

Huang's prescription is to use AI itself to contain AI. He argued the technology can be controlled and deployed safely, and that developers should accelerate the integration of containment technology into AI systems and speed up the development of monitoring technologies, with AI acting as that monitor.

https://x.com/nvidia/status/2110091922337415564

Nvidia is putting computing resources behind that argument in Britain. The company will donate access to advanced computers valued at $250 million over five years — $50 million a year, delivered through UK-based cloud partners — to support research into agentic AI safety and security. A portion will go to BOLD, a lab led by the University of Oxford, to SOFAIR, led by University College London, and to Imperial College London, covering areas including agentic foundation models, safety engineering and robotics safety. Announcing the commitment, Huang said AI capability and safety must advance together. Britain's AI minister, Kanishka Narayan, welcomed the donation, saying it would help ensure future AI is safe and secure.

What It Means

Huang's comments set out, in public, where the world's most important AI chip supplier draws its line: a conversation first, and a cutoff only as a last resort for a customer it judges to be building unsafe software. Because nearly every major AI lab trains on Nvidia hardware, even a hypothetical cutoff policy matters — it signals that access to the industry's essential hardware could, in an extreme case, come with safety conditions attached. For the Indian engineers, researchers and founders who build much of their work on Nvidia systems in the US, the UK and India, the more immediate takeaway is the UK commitment: five years of funded compute for safety research at three leading universities, at a moment when agentic systems are moving from demos into workplaces.

What's Next

Huang continues his European tour with Nvidia's company event in Berlin. The UK research commitment leaves practical details — how compute time will be allocated and which researchers outside the three named institutions can apply — still to be worked out. The wider argument Huang picked, over whether AI development should slow down, is unlikely to settle soon: his answer, delivered in London, is that the industry should speed up the safeguards instead.
